title: Cognitive Set 08: Numbers, Storage DI & Verbal Precision
description: Final aptitude mastery set covering boat-stream ratios, equal-SP profit/loss, HCF-LCM pairs, cuboid diagonal, storage DI, and RC.

questions.question: The ratio of the speed of a boat in still water to the speed of the stream is 5 : 2. The boat takes 4 hours less to travel 84 km downstream than to travel 84 km upstream. What is the speed of the stream?
questions.explanation: Let boat speed = 5k and stream speed = 2k. Then downstream speed = 7k and upstream speed = 3k. Time difference: 84/(3k) - 84/(7k) = 4 => 28/k - 12/k = 4 => 16/k = 4 => k = 4. Stream speed = 2k = 8 km/h.

questions.question: A distributor sells two enterprise laptops at Rs. 49,500 each. On the first he gains 10%, and on the second he loses 10%. What is his overall net profit or loss in rupees?
questions.explanation: Equal SP with +x% and -x% yields an overall loss of (x^2 / 100)% = 1%. Total SP = 2 * 49,500 = Rs. 99,000, which equals 99% of total CP. Thus total CP = Rs. 1,00,000, giving a net loss of 1,00,000 - 99,000 = Rs. 1,000.
questions.shortcut: Overall loss = 1%, so Total SP = 99% of CP => Loss = 99,000 / 99 = Rs. 1,000.

questions.question: The HCF of two 2-digit positive integers is 14 and their LCM is 280. What is the sum of these two integers?
questions.explanation: Let the two numbers be 14a and 14b where gcd(a, b) = 1. Since HCF * LCM = product of numbers, 14 * 280 = 14a * 14b => ab = 20. Coprime pairs for 20 are (1, 20) and (4, 5). Pair (1, 20) gives 14 and 280 (not both 2-digit). Pair (4, 5) gives 56 and 70 (both 2-digit). Sum = 56 + 70 = 126.

questions.question: The ratio of the present ages of Meera and Nisha is 4 : 5. Six years from now, the ratio of their ages will be 5 : 6. What was Meera's age 4 years ago?
questions.explanation: Both ratio terms increase by 1 unit (4->5 and 5->6) over 6 years, so 1 unit = 6 years. Meera's present age = 4 * 6 = 24 years. Four years ago, Meera was 24 - 4 = 20 years old.
questions.shortcut: Equal gap +1 unit = 6 years => Meera now = 24 => 4 years ago = 20.

questions.question: The sum of the first 11 terms of an arithmetic progression is 275. What is the 6th term of this progression?
questions.explanation: For an AP with an odd number of terms n = 11, the sum equals n times the middle term T_((11+1)/2) = T_6. Thus 11 * T_6 = 275 => T_6 = 25.
questions.shortcut: Middle term of 11 terms = average = 275 / 11 = 25.

questions.question: A fair coin is tossed 4 times independently. What is the probability of obtaining at least 3 heads?
questions.explanation: Total outcomes = 2^4 = 16. Favorable outcomes: 3 heads = C(4, 3) = 4 ways, and 4 heads = C(4, 4) = 1 way. Total favorable = 5. Probability = 5/16.

questions.question: An internal server enclosure is a rectangular cuboid measuring 12 cm by 4 cm by 3 cm. What is the length of the longest straight probe that can fit completely inside the enclosure?
questions.explanation: Longest straight line inside a cuboid is its space diagonal: sqrt(12^2 + 4^2 + 3^2) = sqrt(144 + 16 + 9) = sqrt(169) = 13 cm.
questions.shortcut: 3-4-5 gives 5; 5-12-13 gives 13 cm.

questions.question: A bonus pool of Rs. 4,500 is distributed among A, B, and C such that A receives 2/3 of what B receives, and B receives 3/4 of what C receives. How much does A receive?
questions.explanation: Let C = 4 parts => B = (3/4)*4 = 3 parts => A = (2/3)*3 = 2 parts. Ratio A : B : C = 2 : 3 : 4 (sum = 9 parts). A's share = (2 / 9) * 4,500 = Rs. 1,000.

Six panelists—three Architects (A1, A2, A3) and three Engineers (E1, E2, E3)—sit around a circular table facing the center such that no two Architects sit next to each other. A1 sits opposite E2. E1 sits immediately to the right of A1. A3 sits immediately to the right of E1. Who sits immediately to the left of E3?
questions.explanation: Label seats 1..6 counter-clockwise (right = +1, left = -1): set A1 = 1. Opposite A1(1) is E2 = 4. E1 is immediately right (+1) of A1(1) => E1 = 2. A3 is immediately right (+1) of E1(2) => A3 = 3. Remaining Architect seat (odd) is 5 => A2 = 5. Remaining Engineer seat (even) is 6 => E3 = 6. Immediately left (-1) of E3(6) is seat 5 = A2.
questions.shortcut: Counter-clockwise 1..6: [1:A1, 2:E1, 3:A3, 4:E2, 5:A2, 6:E3] => left of E3(6) is A2(5).

questions.question: Statements: (1) No plain-text password is safe. (2) All hashed credentials are salted. (3) Some safe credentials are hashed credentials. Conclusions: I. Some salted credentials are safe. II. No plain-text password is a hashed credential.
questions.explanation: From (3) and (2), the safe credentials that are hashed must also be salted, so some salted credentials are safe (Conclusion I follows). However, hashed credentials are not restricted from overlapping plain-text passwords in the formal syllogism statements alone (Conclusion II does not follow).
questions.shortcut: Safe ∩ Hashed != empty and Hashed ⊆ Salted => Safe ∩ Salted != empty (I follows).

questions.question: Riya, a woman who has no sisters, says, 'Vikram's mother is the only daughter of my mother.' How is Riya related to Vikram?
questions.explanation: Since Riya is a woman with no sisters, 'the only daughter of my mother' refers to Riya herself. Therefore, Vikram's mother is Riya.
questions.shortcut: Only daughter of Riya's mother = Riya => Riya is Vikram's mother.

questions.question: Find the missing term: 8, 12, 24, 60, 180, ?
In a cipher, CLOUD is coded as DNRYI and PROXY is coded as QTRBD. How is TOKEN coded in the same cipher?
questions.explanation: Shift the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, and 5th letters forward by +1, +2, +3, +4, and +5 respectively (wrapping past Z). TOKEN: T+1=U, O+2=Q, K+3=N, E+4=I, N+5=S => UQNIS.
questions.shortcut: Incremental shift +1, +2, +3, +4, +5.

questions.question: Is the area of square S greater than the area of circle C? Statement I: The perimeter of square S equals the circumference of circle C. Statement II: The diagonal of square S equals the diameter of circle C.
options: Either Statement I alone or Statement II alone is sufficient
questions.explanation: From Statement I: For fixed perimeter L, a circle encloses strictly greater area than a square (L^2/(4*pi) > L^2/16), so Area(S) > Area(C) is definitively FALSE (sufficient). From Statement II: Diagonal s*sqrt(2) = 2r => s = r*sqrt(2) => Area(S) = 2*r^2 < pi*r^2 = Area(C), also definitively FALSE (sufficient). Thus either statement alone suffices!
questions.shortcut: Circle has larger area for equal perimeter (I) AND square inscribed in circle has smaller area (II).

questions.question: Node P is 10 km North of Node Q. Node R is 10 km East of Node Q. Node S is 10 km South of Node R. In which direction is Node S with respect to Node P?
questions.explanation: Set Q=(0,0): P=(0,10), R=(10,0), S=(10,-10). Relative to P(0,10), S(10,-10) is 10 km East and 20 km South, which lies in the South-East direction.
questions.shortcut: S is both East (+10) and South (-20) of P => South-East.

questions.question: Situation: Campus placement surveys show 60% of applicants fail the Versant spoken round not due to technical weakness, but due to poor microphone noise cancellation and rushing through repeat-sentence prompts. Which action best addresses this? I. Provide mock acoustic checks and pacing drills before the live test. II. Replace the Versant speaking assessment with a longer trigonometry exam.
questions.explanation: Action I directly mitigates both root causes (hardware audio quality and speaking pace). Action II is irrelevant to spoken English readiness.
questions.shortcut: Directly target mic check + pacing drills (I).

questions.question: Which relationship is best modeled by three concentric circles (inner inside middle inside outer)?
questions.explanation: In relational database theory, every Primary Key is a chosen Candidate Key, and every Candidate Key is a minimal Superkey: Primary Keys ⊂ Candidate Keys ⊂ Superkeys (strictly concentric subsets).
questions.shortcut: Primary Key is a subset of Candidate Keys, which is a subset of Superkeys.

questions.question: Policy: 'To prevent SQL injection across all campus web apps, our security council banned raw string concatenation in database queries and mandated parameterized PreparedStatements.' Which assumption underpins this policy's effectiveness?
options: Developers bind user-supplied parameters via PreparedStatement placeholders rather than concatenating user strings before passing them into PreparedStatement
Parameterized queries execute 10x faster than stored procedures on every engine
All campus web apps run exclusively on relational NoSQL engines
Browser JavaScript frameworks automatically sanitize HTTP headers
questions.explanation: A PreparedStatement only prevents SQL injection if user inputs are passed through `?` placeholders—building the SQL string with `+ userInput` before calling `prepareStatement` still leaves the app vulnerable.
questions.shortcut: PreparedStatement only protects if placeholders are actually used instead of pre-concatenation.

questions.passage: Zero-trust networking rejects the traditional castle-and-moat perimeter model, which trusted any packet already inside a corporate VPN. In cloud-native environments where workloads span public clouds, contractor laptops, and SaaS APIs, a static network perimeter is porous by default. Zero-trust architectures therefore authenticate and authorize every service-to-service call using short-lived cryptographic identities—such as mTLS certificates—regardless of whether the caller sits inside the same subnet or across the public internet.
questions.question: According to the passage, why has the traditional 'castle-and-moat' security model become inadequate?
options: Corporate VPNs encrypt packets too slowly for SaaS APIs
Modern workloads cross external clouds and remote endpoints, eroding any fixed internal perimeter
mTLS certificates cannot function inside a single subnet
Public internet routers strip cryptographic identities from packets
questions.explanation: Sentence 2 notes that because workloads span public clouds, contractor laptops, and SaaS APIs, a static network perimeter is inherently porous.
questions.shortcut: Locate 'static network perimeter is porous by default' and its preceding 'where...' clause.

questions.passage: Zero-trust networking rejects the traditional castle-and-moat perimeter model, which trusted any packet already inside a corporate VPN. In cloud-native environments where workloads span public clouds, contractor laptops, and SaaS APIs, a static network perimeter is porous by default. Zero-trust architectures therefore authenticate and authorize every service-to-service call using short-lived cryptographic identities—such as mTLS certificates—regardless of whether the caller sits inside the same subnet or across the public internet.
questions.question: Under a zero-trust architecture, how should two microservices residing inside the same private subnet communicate?
options: Without authentication, since both are behind the corporate VPN
Using long-lived static IP allowlists without encryption
By authenticating and authorizing each call via short-lived cryptographic identities such as mTLS
By routing all internal calls through contractor laptops
questions.explanation: Sentence 3 explicitly states that zero-trust authenticates and authorizes every call using short-lived cryptographic identities even when the caller sits inside the same subnet.
questions.shortcut: Look at 'regardless of whether the caller sits inside the same subnet'.

questions.question: Identify the erroneous segment: 'The junior developer preferred (A) / debugging the legacy monolith (B) / than rewriting the billing module (C) / from scratch. (D)'
questions.explanation: The verb 'prefer' takes 'to' (not 'than') when comparing two gerunds or nouns: 'preferred debugging ... to rewriting ...'.
questions.shortcut: Always 'prefer X to Y' (never 'prefer X than Y').

questions.question:
Arrange P, Q, R, S in logical sequence:
P. Load balancers detect these failing readiness probes and quietly pull the warming pod out of rotation.
Q. When a Java Spring Boot container starts up, it takes several seconds to initialize connection pools and warm the JIT compiler.
R. Only after the readiness endpoint reports UP does live customer traffic reach the new instance.
S. Routing production requests to the container before initialization completes would trigger immediate 502 errors.
questions.explanation: Q introduces container startup warm-up time. S explains what happens if traffic arrives prematurely ('502 errors'). P explains how readiness probes prevent that. R closes with traffic arriving 'Only after' readiness reports UP. Order: Q-S-P-R.
questions.shortcut: Startup lag (Q) -> Risk if routed early (S) -> Probe protection (P) -> 'Only after' ready (R).

questions.question: Choose the grammatically correct option: 'The lead architect, along with three QA engineers, [are attending] the client architecture review.'
questions.explanation: Phrases introduced by 'along with', 'as well as', or 'together with' are parenthetical and do not make a singular subject plural. The verb agrees with 'The lead architect' => 'is attending'.
questions.shortcut: Ignore 'along with ...' => singular 'The lead architect is attending'.

questions.question: Select the best pair: 'Despite the vendor's ______ assurances of zero downtime, the cutover suffered ______ packet loss for twenty minutes.'
questions.explanation: 'Categorical' (absolute, unconditional) assurances of zero downtime contrast sharply with 'intermittent' (periodic/recurring) packet loss.
questions.shortcut: 'Despite' contrasts absolute promises ('categorical') with actual failures ('intermittent').

questions.question: Spot the grammatical error: 'Please revert back to (A) / the architecture review board (B) / with revised latency benchmarks (C) / by Thursday evening. (D)'
questions.explanation: 'Revert' already means 'return/reply back', so 'revert back' is redundant (and in formal usage, 'reply to' or 'get back to' is preferred over 'revert to').
questions.shortcut: Never pair 'revert' with 'back' (just like 'return back' or 'repeat again').

questions.question:
Order P, Q, R, S coherently:
P. Consequently, read replicas always lag the primary database by a few milliseconds to seconds.
Q. Relational databases typically scale read-heavy dashboards by offloading SELECT queries to asynchronous replicas.
R. Applications that immediately read back a user's just-submitted profile edit from a replica can therefore display stale data.
S. Replication streams ship committed write-ahead log records over the network after the primary transaction commits.
questions.explanation: Q introduces read replicas. S explains how replication ships logs after primary commit. P states the consequence ('Consequently, read replicas always lag'). R states the user-visible bug ('therefore display stale data'). Order: Q-S-P-R.
questions.shortcut: Replicas (Q) -> Log shipping (S) -> Replication lag (P) -> Stale read bug (R).

questions.question: Select the cleanest correction: '[Was the primary key] chosen as a random UUID instead of an auto-incrementing integer, B-tree page splits would increase.'
questions.explanation: In a second-conditional hypothetical inversion ('... would increase'), 'Were + subject + past participle/noun' replaces 'If the primary key were chosen...'.
questions.shortcut: Hypothetical inversion with 'would increase' => 'Were the primary key chosen...'.

questions.question: Statement: 'Every candidate shortlisted for the HCL GET technical panel scored above 75% in the coding round, and no candidate who failed Versant received a final offer.' Given only these facts, which statement MUST be true?
options: Every candidate who scored above 75% in coding received a final offer
Any candidate who received a final offer passed Versant
All candidates who passed Versant were shortlisted for the technical panel
No candidate who failed coding passed Versant
questions.explanation: 'No candidate who failed Versant received a final offer' is equivalent to 'Everyone who received a final offer passed Versant.' The other options commit converse/inverse fallacies.
questions.shortcut: No (~Versant) is Offer => Offer implies Versant.
